blocks.content: Caching is a memory technique with a genuinely different goal from the buffering covered in the previous chapter. Where a buffer absorbs a speed mismatch between two active parties, a cache exists to avoid doing the same expensive work, an expensive read, an expensive computation, more than once, by deliberately keeping a fast copy of data close at hand for reuse.

Caching is not a new idea introduced fresh in this chapter, it has already appeared twice earlier in this course in concrete, specific forms, the TLB in the memory management module and, implicitly, the page cache that keeps recently read disk data available in RAM. This chapter names the general principle behind both.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409610095-643710845.png
1. The Core Idea: Avoid Repeating Expensive Work
blocks.text: 1. The Core Idea: Avoid Repeating Expensive Work

blocks.content: A cache sits between a program and some genuinely slow underlying source of data, a disk, a network connection, a remote server, or even an expensive computation. The first time a specific piece of data is needed, it has to be fetched or computed the slow, expensive way. A cache keeps a copy of that result close at hand, in fast memory, specifically so a later request for the exact same data can be served immediately, without repeating that expensive work at all.

blocks.title: In one sentence
blocks.content: A cache keeps a fast, reusable copy of data or computed results specifically to avoid the cost of repeatedly fetching or recomputing the exact same thing.
2. Caching vs Buffering: A Real, Important Distinction
blocks.text: 2. Caching vs Buffering: A Real, Important Distinction

blocks.content: It is easy to blur caching and buffering together since both involve holding data in memory temporarily, but they solve genuinely different problems. A buffer, covered in the previous chapter, absorbs a speed mismatch between an active producer and an active consumer, data typically flows through it once, on its way somewhere.

A cache instead deliberately keeps data around specifically so it can be reused later, the same piece of data being requested a second or third time is exactly the scenario a cache is built to make fast. This distinction, flowing through once versus deliberately kept for reuse, is the cleanest way to tell the two apart.

blocks.alt: Caching vs Buffering: A Real, Important Distinction

3. Cache Hits and Misses

Every cache lookup resolves to exactly one of two outcomes. A cache hit means the requested data is already sitting in the cache, and it can be returned immediately with no access to the slow underlying source needed at all. A cache miss means the data is not currently cached, forcing an access to the slow source, after which a copy is typically stored in the cache so a future request for that same data becomes a hit instead.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409610096-186604972.png
4. Caching, Already Seen Twice in This Course
blocks.text: 4. Caching, Already Seen Twice in This Course

blocks.content: The TLB, covered in complete depth in the memory management module, is precisely a cache, a fast, small store of recently used page table translations, specifically to avoid the cost of a full page table walk on every single memory access. Every hit and miss concept from this chapter applies directly, a TLB hit skips the full translation, a TLB miss falls back to walking the actual page table.

The disk page cache, briefly implicit in earlier file systems chapters, works the same way for disk data: recently read disk blocks are kept in RAM, so a program reading the same file data again shortly afterward is served directly from fast RAM rather than triggering another genuinely slow disk access.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409610096-532186848.png
blocks.alt: Caching, Already Seen Twice in This Course

blocks.content: 5. Cache Eviction: The Same Problem as Page Replacement
blocks.text: 5. Cache Eviction: The Same Problem as Page Replacement

blocks.content: A cache, exactly like physical RAM in the page replacement module, has finite capacity. When it is full and new data needs to be cached, something existing has to be evicted to make room, and deciding which entry to evict is, structurally, the exact same problem the page replacement algorithms module solved for evicting resident pages.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409610096-153857649.png
blocks.alt: Cache Eviction: The Same Problem as Page Replacement

blocks.content: This is not a coincidence or a loose analogy, it is the same underlying problem wearing a different name. LRU, covered in full in that module, is a genuinely common real world cache eviction policy for exactly the reason established there, it tends to keep the data most likely to be reused, based on locality of reference, resident.
6. Write Through vs Write Back Caching
blocks.text: 6. Write Through vs Write Back Caching

blocks.content: Caching gets more subtle the moment writes, not just reads, are involved, since a cached copy and the underlying slow source can now genuinely disagree with each other. Write through caching updates both the cache and the underlying slow source together, immediately, on every single write, guaranteeing they never diverge, at the real cost of every write paying the slow source cost directly.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409610096-331682442.png
blocks.alt: Write Through vs Write Back Caching

blocks.content: Write back caching instead updates only the cache immediately, marking that entry dirty, and defers actually writing it back to the slow underlying source until later, batching many writes together for genuinely better performance. The real, honest cost is a real data loss risk: if the system crashes before a dirty entry is actually written back, that update is lost entirely.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409610096-138419189.png
blocks.alt: Write Through vs Write Back Caching

blocks.content: {"headers":["Policy","Write speed","Risk if the system crashes"],"rows":[["Write through","Slower, every write pays the full source cost","None, cache and source never diverge"],["Write back","Faster, writes are batched and deferred","Real, any unwritten dirty data is lost"]]}
7. A Concrete Example: The Disk Page Cache in Action
blocks.text: 7. A Concrete Example: The Disk Page Cache in Action

blocks.content: Tracing one concrete example ties this together. A program reads a specific disk block for the first time, a genuine cache miss, triggering a real, comparatively slow disk access. The operating system keeps a copy of that block in a page cache living in RAM. If that same program, or even a different program, reads the exact same block again shortly afterward, it is served directly from RAM, a cache hit, with no disk access needed at all.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409610097-159452125.png
blocks.alt: A Concrete Example: The Disk Page Cache in Action

blocks.content: 8. Common Mistakes and Interview Angle

["Confusing a cache with a buffer simply because both temporarily hold data in memory, when they solve genuinely different problems, speed mismatch absorption versus avoiding repeated expensive work.","Assuming write back caching is always the better choice purely because it is faster, without weighing its real, honest data loss risk if a crash happens before dirty data is written back.","Not recognizing the TLB and the disk page cache, both already covered earlier in this course, as concrete, specific instances of the exact same general caching principle covered in this chapter."]
items: Confusing a cache with a buffer simply because both temporarily hold data in memory, when they solve genuinely different problems, speed mismatch absorption versus avoiding repeated expensive work.
Assuming write back caching is always the better choice purely because it is faster, without weighing its real, honest data loss risk if a crash happens before dirty data is written back.
Not recognizing the TLB and the disk page cache, both already covered earlier in this course, as concrete, specific instances of the exact same general caching principle covered in this chapter.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.content: Be ready to distinguish caching from buffering precisely, to explain write through versus write back with their real tradeoffs, and to explicitly connect cache eviction back to the page replacement algorithms module as the exact same underlying problem.

With buffering and caching both covered, the final chapter in this module covers spooling, a related technique specifically for coordinating access to a slow device that can only serve one request at a time.
